steps.text: In the first week at university a symbol appears that hardly came up at school: the capital Greek sigma \(\Sigma\). It is nothing but an abbreviation – but one you must be able to read and write fluently.
steps.explanation:
Our roadmap:
1. Reading and writing the summation sign
2. Rules – and what is NOT allowed
3. Index shifts and telescoping sums
4. The most important sum formulas
5. Product sign, factorial and binomial coefficient
steps.insight: \(\Sigma\) stands for "sum", \(\Pi\) for "product". Both are just shorthand for long expressions.

steps.text: The summation sign combines many summands of the same shape:
steps.explanation:
How to read it:
• \(k\) is the index of summation.
• Below is the start value (\(k = 1\)), above the end value (\(5\)).
• On the right is the term into which you substitute \(k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\) one after another.
• All results are added.

The animation shows the sum "unrolling" step by step.
steps.insight: Read aloud: "sum over \(k\) from \(1\) to \(5\) of \(k\) squared". When reading, always look at the bounds first.

steps.text: Three observations that often cause confusion:
steps.explanation:
• The name of the index doesn't matter: \(k\), \(i\) or \(j\) – the result is the same. It only exists inside the sum.
• The number of summands is end value \(-\) start value \(+ 1\). From \(3\) to \(7\) there are \(5\) summands, not \(4\)!
• If the term does not depend on \(k\) at all, the constant is simply added that many times: \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} 3 = 3n\), not \(3\).
steps.insight: The upper bound may be a variable, e.g. \(n\). Then the result is a term in \(n\) – exactly the kind of formula you later prove by induction.

steps.text: The other way round: bring a written-out sum into \(\Sigma\) notation. Look for the rule that builds the \(k\)-th summand.
steps.explanation:
Procedure:
1. What changes from summand to summand? (multiples of \(3\), powers of two, …)
2. Set up a formula for the \(k\)-th summand.
3. Determine the bounds: for which \(k\) do you get the first, for which the last summand? (\(3k = 30 \Rightarrow k = 10\))

Alternating signs are produced with \((-1)^k\) or \((-1)^{k+1}\) – depending on whether the first summand should be negative or positive.
steps.insight: Check: substitute the bounds into your formula and verify that the first and last summands are right.

steps.text: Since a sum is just a long addition, the familiar arithmetic laws apply – in sum notation they look like this:
steps.explanation:
• Line 1 (commutative and associative laws): sums may be split.
• Line 2 (distributive law): constant factors may be pulled out.
• Line 3: a sum may be split at some position \(m\).

Example: \(\sum_{k=1}^{10} (2k + 1)\) \(= 2\sum_{k=1}^{10} k + \sum_{k=1}^{10} 1\) \(= 2 \cdot 55 + 10 = 120\).
steps.insight: You may only pull out what does NOT depend on \(k\): \(\sum_{k} k \cdot a_k \neq k \sum_{k} a_k\) – outside the sum there is no \(k\) at all!

steps.text: Just as important is what does NOT hold. These mistakes show up in exams all the time:
steps.explanation:
Counterexamples with \(n = 2\), \(a_k = b_k = k\):
• \(1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2 = 5\), but \((1 + 2)(1 + 2) = 9\).
• The second line is the same example.
• \((1 + 1) + (2 + 1) = 5\), but \((1 + 2) + 1 = 4\). Correct: \(\sum (a_k + 1) = \sum a_k + n\).

The reason: expanding \((a_1 + a_2)(b_1 + b_2)\) also produces the "mixed" products \(a_1 b_2\) and \(a_2 b_1\).
steps.insight: When in doubt: write out the sum with \(n = 2\) and compare. That exposes almost every wrong rule.

steps.text: An index shift changes the bounds and the term so that the same summands appear. Example: set \(j = k - 1\).
steps.explanation:
Recipe for \(j = k - 2\):
1. Convert the bounds: \(k = 3 \Rightarrow j = 1\), \(k = 8 \Rightarrow j = 6\).
2. Replace \(k\) in the term: \(k = j + 2\), so \((k - 2)^2 = j^2\).

Check: both sums have \(6\) summands: \(1^2 + 2^2 + \ldots + 6^2 = 91\).

What for? To combine two sums with the same index, or to apply a known formula (e.g. one starting at \(k = 1\)).
steps.section: Chapter 3 · Index shifts and telescoping sums
steps.insight: If the index in the term increases by \(c\), the bounds decrease by \(c\) – and vice versa. The number of summands always stays the same.

steps.text: A particularly nice trick: telescoping sums. If the summands are differences of consecutive terms, almost all of them cancel.
steps.explanation:
Written out:
\(\left(1 - \frac{1}{2}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}\right) + \ldots + \left(\frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n+1}\right)\).

Every \(-\frac{1}{k+1}\) is wiped out by the \(+\frac{1}{k+1}\) of the next summand. Only the very first and the very last term survive – like a telescope being collapsed.

In general: \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} (b_k - b_{k+1}) = b_1 - b_{n+1}\).
steps.section: Chapter 3 · Index shifts and telescoping sums
steps.insight: Telescoping sums are THE tool for computing series exactly in calculus. Often the difference form has to be created first with fraction arithmetic: \(\frac{1}{k(k+1)} = \frac{1}{k} - \frac{1}{k+1}\).

steps.text: You should know three sum formulas. The first goes back to the young Gauss:
steps.explanation:
Idea: write the sum twice – once forwards, once backwards – and add column by column:
\(1 + n\), \(2 + (n - 1)\), …, every column gives \(n + 1\). There are \(n\) columns, so \(2S = n(n+1)\).

The animation shows the same geometrically: two "staircases" form a rectangle.

Example: \(1 + 2 + \ldots + 100 = \frac{100 \cdot 101}{2} = 5050\).
steps.insight: The sum of the first \(n\) numbers is "count times mean": \(n \cdot \frac{1 + n}{2}\). This works for every arithmetic sequence.

steps.explanation:
The sum of squares: for \(n = 3\), \(1 + 4 + 9 = 14\), and \(\frac{3 \cdot 4 \cdot 7}{6} = 14\) ✓.

The geometric sum is the most important. Derivation: let \(S = 1 + q + \ldots + q^n\). Then \(qS = q + q^2 + \ldots + q^{n+1}\). Subtracting leaves only \(qS - S = q^{n+1} - 1\) – almost everything cancels (a telescope again!).

Example: \(1 + 2 + 4 + \ldots + 512 = \sum_{k=0}^{9} 2^k = \frac{2^{10} - 1}{2 - 1} = 1023\).
steps.insight: The geometric sum is the key to interest calculations, geometric series and convergence proofs. Remember the derivation, not the formula!

steps.text: Analogous to the summation sign there is the product sign \(\Pi\) (capital pi):
steps.formula: \prod_{k=1}^{n} a_k = a_1 \cdot a_2 \cdot \ldots \cdot a_n, \qquad n! = \prod_{k=1}^{n} k = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot \ldots \cdot n
steps.explanation:
The most important product is the factorial \(n!\) ("\(n\) factorial"):
\(3! = 6\), \(\;5! = 120\), \(\;10! = 3\,628\,800\). By convention \(0! = 1\) (empty product).

Factorials grow extremely fast. So when calculating, cancel instead of computing:
\(\frac{7!}{5!} = \frac{7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5!}{5!} = 42\), \(\;\frac{(n+1)!}{n!} = n + 1\).

\(n!\) counts the number of ways to arrange \(n\) objects in a row.
steps.insight: Useful: \((n+1)! = (n+1) \cdot n!\). With this almost every fraction of factorials can be cancelled.

steps.text: From factorials one builds the binomial coefficient ("\(n\) choose \(k\)"):
steps.explanation:
\(\binom{n}{k}\) counts the number of ways to choose \(k\) objects from \(n\) (without order). Example lottery: \(\binom{49}{6} = 13\,983\,816\).

Calculation trick: \(k\) factors counting down on top, \(k!\) below:
\(\binom{8}{3} = \frac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6}{3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} = 56\).

Properties:
• \(\binom{n}{0} = \binom{n}{n} = 1\), \(\;\binom{n}{1} = n\)
• Symmetry: \(\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}\)
• Pascal's rule: \(\binom{n}{k} + \binom{n}{k+1} = \binom{n+1}{k+1}\)
steps.insight: With the summation sign and binomial coefficients, the binomial theorem reads compactly: \((a + b)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} a^{n-k} b^k\).

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. Read and write \(\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k\). Number of summands: \(n - m + 1\).

2. Split sums, pull out constants, split at a position. But: \(\sum a_k b_k \neq \sum a_k \cdot \sum b_k\).

3. Index shift: adjust bounds and term together. Telescoping sums: \(\sum (b_k - b_{k+1}) = b_1 - b_{n+1}\).

4. \(\sum k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\), \(\sum k^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\), \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} q^k = \frac{q^{n+1} - 1}{q - 1}\).

5. \(\prod\), \(n!\) with \(0! = 1\), \(\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}\).
steps.insight: Congratulations! This notation returns in "Mathematical Induction" (proving sum formulas), "Sequences and Series" (infinite sums) and "Matrices" (matrix product).
